passage: I'm Manoj, the neighbour in 4B, and I only know what I saw. For weeks Dhruv's partner had been the subject of low voices on the landing, something about a promise that got broken. I don't know all of it. On Sunday I was carrying vegetables up the stairs when I heard Dhruv on the half-landing, speaking quietly: "I've decided to forgive you. It won't happen with one sentence, and it won't be quick. But I need you to tell me before you make plans that involve us." Dhruv's partner said something I couldn't catch. Dhruv's hands were shaking a little on the railing, and Dhruv didn't hug, didn't shout. Just nodded and went in. I couldn't tell whether that was peace or exhaustion, honestly.

qa.q: Where was Dhruv standing when speaking to the partner?
qa.a: On the half-landing of the stairs.

qa.q: What does Dhruv want, judging from what Manoj overheard?
qa.a: Dhruv wants to let go of the anger, but also wants the partner to tell Dhruv before making plans that involve them both, so forgiving does not mean pretending nothing happened.

qa.q: What makes Dhruv's approach a mature one, in your view?
qa.a: It sets forgiveness as a decision that will take time, not one sentence, and states what must change. Nothing is buried or forgotten.

qa.q: How sure can Manoj be about Dhruv's inner state?
qa.a: Not very sure. Manoj saw shaking hands and a nod, and admits not knowing whether it was peace or exhaustion.

grounding: Shows the protagonist deciding to forgive a partner for a real wound, saying it will take time and stating what must change, seen by an observer who cannot know their inner state.

passage:
June. Dolma found out that Raghav had told his whole family about her miscarriage at a Sunday lunch, without asking her. She had wanted to tell them herself, or not at all. For a week she barely spoke to him. At night she lay awake, rehearsing all the ways she could hurt him back.

July, a Saturday. Raghav had apologised many times. That morning Dolma decided: I am going to forgive him. She told him, and felt the weight shift, a little. Only a little. "This isn't one sentence. It will take time."

August. They sat at the table and she said, calmly, "I've let go of wanting to punish you. But things need to change. Anything about my body, my health, you ask me first. Always." Raghav nodded. He wrote it on a note and stuck it on the fridge. Some mornings she still felt the old hurt. But the revenge speeches had stopped.

qa.q: What did Raghav tell his family without asking Dolma?
qa.a: Raghav told his family about her miscarriage at a Sunday lunch.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling in June?
qa.a: Dolma felt deeply betrayed and angry, lying awake rehearsing ways to hurt him back.

qa.q: What did Dolma's forgiveness include, and why does it matter?
qa.a: It included letting go of revenge while clearly stating what must change, so forgiveness didn't mean pretending nothing happened.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel when Dolma states the new rule?
qa.a: Raghav likely feels relieved to be forgiven and serious about change, which is why he writes the rule on the fridge.

grounding: The three beats show a young wife forgiving a real wound over time, letting go of revenge while stating what must change.

passage:
Akash, you're asking how your grandfather and I stayed married fifty years? Let me, your Alka dadi, tell you the part nobody tells you. When I was twenty-five, your dada borrowed money from my father without telling me, and lost it in a business with his friend. My father had to sell land. I found out from my mother.

I was so angry I packed a bag. I stayed with my sister a month. Every night I thought of ways to shame him in front of his family.

Then I decided to forgive him. Not because he deserved it that day. Because I didn't want revenge to eat me. But I told him: forgiving does not mean forgetting. From now on, no money decision without me. And you will tell my father yourself what you did.

He did. It took years before I trusted him fully. Forgiveness was a road, beta, not a door.

qa.q: How long did Alka stay with her sister?
qa.a: She stayed with her sister a month.

qa.q: How did young Alka feel when she found out about the money?
qa.a: Young Alka felt furious and betrayed, packing a bag and thinking of ways to shame him.

qa.q: What choice in the story made forgiveness real rather than pretending?
qa.a: Alka decided to let go of revenge while setting clear conditions: no money decisions without her, and he must tell her father himself.

qa.q: How might Alka's father have felt when her husband told him the truth?
qa.a: Her father may have felt hurt and angry, but perhaps also some respect that the young man faced him honestly.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young wife forgiving a real wound over years, letting go of revenge while stating what must change.
